title: McClave Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: McClave wells have a 35 ft median depth, with finished-well costs commonly modeled at $7,200-$13,900.
h1: McClave, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near McClave means looking closely at the well record, not just the asking price. Permits within 5 miles show a shallow local pattern overall, but the spread is wide: some wells go much deeper than the typical plains well. The records also show strong reported yields, although only a small share of wells include a pump-yield result.

This page covers permitted wells around McClave, including nearby Hasty and Wiley, and puts the local numbers into practical terms for a buyer, builder, or landowner.

sections.heading: McClave wells are usually shallow, but the range is wide
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near McClave is 35 feet. The middle half runs from 12 to 156 feet, so a typical drilling estimate may be based on a shallow alluvial well, but the local record does not guarantee that result. About 73% of wells are under 100 feet. Another 6% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 14% between 300 and 600 feet, and 6% reach 600 feet or more.

The deepest recorded well is 720 feet, and the 90th-percentile depth is 515 feet. McClave sits in plains terrain with alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. That setting can produce shallow wells, while local geology and the intended aquifer still control the final depth.

sections.heading: Reported yields look strong, with limited testing records
sections.html:
Only 27 wells in the records report a pump yield, so treat the yield statistics as useful local evidence rather than a promise for a particular lot. Among those reports, the median yield is 25.6 gallons per minute, and the middle half ranges from 15.0 to 460.5 gallons per minute.

No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, and none fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. About 22% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 78% report more than 15 gallons per minute. That is favorable for ordinary household use, but a buyer should still request the actual well construction and pump records. An exempt household-use well is generally subject to a 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and higher-demand plans may require different water-rights work.

sections.heading: The water-level record is too thin to prove a trend
sections.html:
Six wells report a static water level, with a median depth to water of 21 feet. The middle half ranges from 14 to 181 feet. That spread matters when planning casing, pump setting, trenching, and electrical work, but it is not enough to describe every lot around McClave.

The available water-level records do not establish a dropping or rising water table. There are too few reported measurements, and the facts do not provide a time series by decade. A static water level is also different from the pumping level while the well is being used. Before closing, ask for the well permit, well construction report, static level, pump test, and any recent service information. Compare nearby records in McClave, Hasty, Wiley, and the surrounding Bent County plains rather than relying on one well.

sections.heading: Permit activity grew in the 2000s, with records through 2023
sections.html:
The permit history shows wells permitted in every decade from the 1950s through the 2020s. Records include 9 permits in the 1950s, 5 in the 1960s, 13 in the 1970s, 17 in the 1980s, and 23 in the 1990s. The largest decade is the 2000s, with 71 permits. There are 9 in the 2010s and 10 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2023.

The most active drillers named in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 37 wells; Hoffman (Hoffman, Earl), with 21; and Ark Valley Pump & Supply (Smith, William David), with 11. These names help with record searches, but they do not tell you who is available for a new job today. Verify current licensing, insurance, scope, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: A median-depth McClave well models at $7,200 to $13,900 finished
sections.html:
For McClave's alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses about $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 35 feet, that puts the drilled hole at roughly $1,200 to $1,900. That is only the hole, not a functioning water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $7,200 to $13,900 at the median depth. A deeper-than-typical site, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, water treatment, or a longer utility run can change the bid. Ask each contractor to separate drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, testing, trenching, electrical, permits, and abandonment risk. Because 27 wells report a pump yield while 159 report a total depth, the cost estimate should not be treated as a guaranteed water result.

sections.heading: Check PFAS, low-yield risk, septic space, and building plans
sections.html:
Environmental due diligence matters around McClave. Mapping shows 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, along with 2 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped area. Those figures do not determine water quality at a particular parcel. Test the well for ordinary drinking-water concerns and ask the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment or local officials about any nearby PFAS information.

Low yield is not the only risk. A dry hole, poor construction, inadequate casing or grout, pump failure, and septic setbacks can affect a buildable lot. Confirm the DWR permit and permitted use. Domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells make up different portions of the record, so a nearby irrigation well is not proof that a household-use permit is available. Check augmentation requirements if the proposed use affects an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Buy the lot after checking the actual well file
sections.html:
Before buying near McClave, start with the Colorado Division of Water Resources permit and well construction records. Of 228 wells in the five-mile dataset, 154 are recorded as constructed and 159 report a total depth. That means some map points have incomplete information. Use nearby wells as a screening tool, then have a driller evaluate the parcel itself.

For an existing home, obtain the pump test, recent water-quality results, pressure-tank information, and repair history. For vacant land, confirm access for a rig, likely drilling location, septic layout, electrical route, and the legal water use before spending on design. A shallow local median is helpful for budgeting, but the record reaching 720 feet shows why a fixed-depth promise is unsafe. If the property is near Wiley, Hasty, Lamar, Las Animas, or Eads, use those areas only as additional context, not as a substitute for parcel-specific investigation.

faq.q: How deep are wells in McClave, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of McClave is 35 feet. The middle half runs from 12 to 156 feet, and 73% are under 100 feet. Depth is not uniform: the 90th percentile is 515 feet and the deepest recorded well is 720 feet. A driller should review nearby construction records before bidding your parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in McClave?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $1,200-$1,900. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $7,200-$13,900. Deeper drilling, access, casing, grout, treatment, and longer utility runs can change the final price.

faq.q: How much water do McClave wells produce?
faq.a: Only 27 wells report a pump yield, so the yield data is limited. Those reports have a median of 25.6 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 15.0 to 460.5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 5 gallons per minute. Confirm the actual pump test and permitted use; a nearby result is not a guarantee for your lot.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in McClave?
faq.a: The well records do not establish drinking-water safety. Mapping shows 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, plus 2 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing or new household well, especially for PFAS and standard drinking-water concerns, and review local environmental information before relying on the water.

faq.q: Are there water-rights issues with a well near McClave?
faq.a: The records include domestic or household, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells, so the permit type matters. Confirm the DWR permit and its allowed use before buying or building. Exempt household-use wells generally have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. If the proposed use is in an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan or other water-rights review may be required.
